case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: Standing doctrine has tightened since, and TransUnion requires the concrete-harm analysis claim by claim, so Patel anchors face-template cases without automatically carrying every downstream BIPA theory.
case.holding: Creating face templates from photographs without BIPA's notice and consent is a concrete injury conferring Article III standing, because the statute protects a substantive privacy interest, not a procedural formality.

live_cases.name: Miller v. Clearview AI "Artificial Intelligence" Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The federal companion to Rosenbach: it keeps biometric class actions in federal court by holding that unconsented face-scanning is real harm. Every face and voice embedding pipeline trained on personal media is measured against the exposure this case certified.

reading.body:
Patel established that creating face templates from photographs without consent is a concrete injury under federal law, allowing biometric privacy lawsuits to proceed in federal court.

The case turned on whether a procedural violation—failing to notify someone before scanning their face—creates a real harm that courts can remedy. The Ninth Circuit held that it does. The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act protects something substantive: control over your own facial geometry. Extracting that geometry and storing it as a template without permission violates that right, regardless of whether you can prove the template was ever misused. This reasoning anchors every subsequent face-template case brought in federal court.

For AI systems, this holding measures exposure. Every face embedding pipeline trained on personal photographs without explicit consent—from social media archives to scrape-trained vision models—operates in the shadow of Patel. Companies cannot defend the practice by claiming they merely extracted data or that no individual harm occurred. The court certified that the extraction itself is the harm.

The case does not resolve what happens downstream. It does not require proof that a template was sold, matched against a database, or used to identify someone without consent. It does not govern voice embeddings, facial recognition accuracy, or the business models built on biometric data. It does not prevent face-scanning with consent. Later cases citing it, including against Clearview AI, test whether those downstream uses add separate injuries or whether Patel's foundation suffices to hold liability.
